title: Three Lessons Learned From Coaching Teachers
author: Sarah Cottinghatt
summary: Sarah Cottinghatt tells three stories from her coaching practice, each teaching a different lesson about mistaken assumptions coaches make. In the first, she spends weeks trying to get a teacher named Jack to insist on silence before speaking, assuming he simply hadn't honed the technique, until she finally asks why he doesn't seem to mind students talking and learns his real decision-driver ('they're teenagers, they talk') was never going to disappear, only be channelled into planned moments for talk. In the second, drawing on Chesterton's fence, she nearly coaches a trainee named Anna out of an unusual silent-and-support approach before learning it was a deliberate, successful response to her most challenging class, a mistake Cottinghatt attributes to coaches seeing less than one percent of a teacher's actual teaching and wrongly assuming their own mental model matches the teacher's. In the third, she generalises across many schools she's worked with: teachers doing the right techniques at the wrong time, more consistency but no escape from a compliance model, uncertainty about training coaches to spot what matters, all pointing to the same root cause, training that focuses on actions without training the decision-making (judgement) that should drive when those actions are used. She closes arguing that surfacing a teacher's reasoning, not just their visible technique, is the only way out of a 'process problem' that more process can't solve.
points: Cottinghatt's Jack story shows a coach mistaking a stable decision-driver ('teenagers talk, it's natural') for an unhoned skill, and reframes the fix as channelling the driver into planned moments rather than fighting it directly.

Her Anna story, framed through Chesterton's fence, shows a successful but unconventional teaching approach (silence-and-support for a genuinely difficult class) nearly getting 'corrected' away by a coach who assumed her own mental model matched the teacher's.

She quantifies the epistemic humility her role requires: coaches typically see well under one percent of a teacher's actual teaching, which she argues should make coaches hold their pre-session hunches lightly rather than treating them as diagnoses.

Her generalised pattern across many schools, right technique wrong time, more consistency but stuck in compliance, uncertainty about training coaches, all trace to training actions without training the judgement that should govern when to use them.
quotes: He said 'They're teenagers. They talk. When I was a teenager, I couldn't help myself, it's natural.' And looking back, this was the turning point.
My big mistake was that I’d assumed Jack and I were on the same page about the situation: I assumed he knew he had to get silence but just hadn’t honed his practice enough to do it.
There's a rule of thumb people talk about, Chesterton's fence. If there's a fence, don't remove it until you understand why it was put there in the first place.
She’d worked hard to get them to pay attention and learn. Eventually, she resorted to what she called ‘silence and support’ and results had been brilliant.

Coaches see usually >1% of a teacher's teaching. This, coupled with the fact that we all perceive the same situations in at least slightly different ways, means we need to check the assumptions we are making.
When we train teachers by focusing on actions, we get overgeneralised actions. They won’t be done at the right time for the right reason.
